We coupled the dietary differences results with vegetation structure and traffic density records to assess the effects of human activity intensity and infrastructure on dietary composition. Before the anthropause, roadside populations consumed dicot‐rich diets distinct from nearby undisturbed meadow populations. During the reduced human activity of the anthropause, roadside pika diets rapidly converged with those of undisturbed populations within a single year, decoupling from local roadside vegetation compositions. After human activity resumed, dietary divergence between roadside and natural populations reappeared slowly across generations. These data reveal an asymmetric, multigenerational response: rapid convergence under reduced disturbance, followed by a slow divergence with the resumption of disturbance. Regression analyses show that traffic density was associated with dietary divergence between habitats and with diet–vegetation dissimilarity in roadside populations. These multigenerational data demonstrate that wildlife in human‐modified landscapes remain sensitive to changes in human activity, even after prolonged exposure. Importantly, these asymmetric responses suggest that temporary reductions in human disturbance, such as traffic management, can yield lasting biodiversity benefits in increasingly human‐dominated landscapes, and these responses should be explored as part of broader conservation efforts in human‐modified ecosystems. 中文摘要 人类活动强度的动态变化深刻影响着野生动物的行为与资源利用，但长期生活在人类干扰环境中的动物如何响应干扰强度的起伏，目前仍缺乏长期、连续的实证证据。新冠疫情防控期间人类活动的大幅减少（即“人类活动暂停”，Anthropause），为检验野生动物对干扰强度变化的响应机制提供了一个难得的准实验条件。 本研究以青藏高原代表性小型哺乳动物鼠兔（Ochotona spp.）为研究对象，整合 2018—2024 年连续 7 年的监测数据，系统对比了新冠疫情防控（跨城人员流动受限期）之前（2018—2019 年）、期间（2020—2022 年）和之后（2023—2024 年）公路沿线种群与远离道路草甸种群的食性差异。研究基于粪便 DNA 宏条形码技术测定鼠兔食性，并结合同期植被组成和交通流量数据，深入解析食性动态与人类活动强度之间的定量关系。 研究发现，疫情前路边鼠兔种群食性以双子叶植物为主，与邻近草甸种群存在显著分化。疫情期间，随着人类活动大幅减少，路边种群的食性在短短一个世代内迅速向草甸种群趋同，同时与其所在路边的植被组成拉大了差异；而在疫情后人类活动恢复常态时，路边种群食性并未随之迅速复原，而是经历了数个世代才缓慢恢复至疫情前的分化状态。 这种响应呈现出显著的不对称性：对干扰减弱的响应极为迅速，而对干扰恢复的响应则明显滞后。机制分析进一步表明，交通流量越大，路边与草甸种群间的食性分化越显著，且路边种群的食性越趋近于当地路边植被组成。 这项长达 7 年的连续监测表明，即使长期生活在人类改造环境中的野生动物，其资源利用策略仍具备高度的可塑性，且对干扰“消退”与“重现”的响应具有非对称特征。这一发现意味着，阶段性或周期性地降低交通等人类干扰，能够产生比干扰暂停期本身更持久的生态效应，为人类主导景观下的野生动物保护与管理提供了新的科学思路。
n761aa205acca: Distinct waterbird species influence nutrient cycling through guano contributions in Great Lakes coastal wetlands. Waterbird‐derived nutrients favour distinct algal communities and wetland sediments rapidly remove waterbird nutrients via biogeochemical processes. These contributions may be locally important during nutrient‐limiting times, but the magnitude of nutrients contributed depends on wetland management strategy. Abstract Freshwater wetlands along the Laurentian Great Lakes provide vital ecosystem services, two of which include providing habitat for millions of waterfowl and reducing nutrient (nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P)) runoff from the landscape. Nutrient bioavailability in wetlands is influenced by waterbirds, which shape biogeochemical dynamics through the excretion of N‐ and P‐rich guano. There has been limited focus on how waterbirds shape nutrient budgets (i.e. via zoogeochemical effects) in wetlands that are managed for both waterfowl habitat and nutrient retention. Therefore, we examined how three distinct functional groups of common waterbirds influence nutrient biogeochemistry and algal community structure in two coastal freshwater wetlands along Lake Erie (Ohio, USA). We experimentally measured how waterbird‐derived nutrient contributions shape wetland nutrient removal and elicit changes in algal community composition through experimental additions of guano to microcosms. We collected biweekly waterbird densities throughout 1 year and used guano nutrient content and dropping rates to estimate annual waterbird N and P fluxes. We then assessed the relative importance of waterbird‐nutrient contributions through comparisons to previously monitored net nutrient loads from landscape runoff. Waterbird guano additions initially increased nutrient concentrations in microcosms; however, wetland sediments rapidly removed most of the total P, but only approximately half of the total N from the water column. Waterbird guano from different functional groups favoured distinct algal communities, driven primarily by differences in guano total N content. Waterbird‐derived nutrient fluxes were highest during fall migration and may be locally important in wetlands during nutrient‐limiting times. However, annual waterbird‐derived nutrient fluxes are often negligible (<1.3%) compared with external loads from surrounding agriculture‐dominated watersheds. By understanding the zoogeochemical effects that waterbirds have in freshwaters, we can inform management decisions that simultaneously protect waterfowl habitat and enhance nutrient removal processes to maximize multiple ecosystem services in the Great Lakes region.
nc2ee71f0c50a: ‘malddaba’ is a new open‐access database that compiles age‐specific demographic rates, such as survival and reproduction, for wild mammals. The database currently contains over 638 records of age‐ and sex‐specific demographic rates for 174 species of mammal. It is available online to any researcher interested in comparative analyses in evolutionary biology and demography. Abstract The question of how individual age influences demographic transition rates, such as survival probabilities and reproduction rates, has long been a main question for demographers and evolutionary ecologists. This has resulted in the accumulation of studies estimating the age‐specific demographic transition rates across the tree of life over the last few decades. Although this accumulation of studies has enabled comparative demographic analyses to be developed, such analyses remain difficult to perform because age‐specific data are scattered across literature. Here, we present a new open‐access database, malddaba, which compiles age‐specific demographic rates for mammals in the wild from published information. Currently, the database encompasses 174 species from 255 publications, representing 437 age‐ and sex‐specific survival series and 201 age‐ and sex‐specific reproduction series. Each series is reported using a standardized approach aimed at facilitating the extraction and use of that dataset by anyone interested in comparative evolutionary biology and demography. We show how malddaba can be used to address a variety of questions, ranging from comparative ageing with the assessment of actuarial and reproductive senescence patterns in a wide diversity of mammals to comparative population dynamics. For this purpose, in addition to the raw demographic rate records, we were able to build 45 population‐specific life tables using malddaba records, which allow demographic outputs to be estimated accurately, such as population growth rate and generation time for those species. The malddaba database will be regularly updated to keep adding new demographic estimates and bring a comprehensive and dynamic view of the diversity of demographic trajectories across mammals.
n85cc146761af: Opportunistic surveys, such as those archived by citizen science biodiversity inventory programs, can provide species observations over large spans of space and time. Like most biodiversity data, opportunistic reports suffer from imperfect detection of organisms, which can distort species distribution models used for science and natural resource management. Occupancy models and their variants account for imperfect detection, but opportunistic surveys are usually not collected using the sampling protocols required for occupancy modelling. The Site Clustering Problem addresses this issue by formulating the construction of sites from unstructured observations as a clustering task. We developed and evaluated a workflow for building occupancy models from opportunistic data, comprised of steps to cluster observations, form site geometries and fit models. We compared eight clustering approaches as potential solutions to the Site Clustering Problem on 31 avian species in Oregon, USA. We evaluated the clustering approaches based on predictive performance of the downstream occupancy models and analysed the impact of species traits such as home range size and habitat type on the results. In simulation studies, we measured the difference between estimated parameters and true data‐generating parameters. Our evaluation revealed several insights. Clustering methods from machine learning that accounted for similarity in both environmental and geographic space allowed observations from nearby geospatial coordinates in similar environments to be grouped together, and some of these methods were top performers. That said, the simple approach of grouping two to ten co‐located observations as sites was also competitive. This study explored a set of options for bridging the gap between large databases of opportunistic biodiversity surveys and the sampling frameworks underlying models that correct for imperfect detection of organisms. Our results provide preliminary guidance for modellers seeking to create sites for occupancy models as well as directions for future work. In particular, we expect that the development of clustering approaches that can consider species‐specific spatial constraints will improve solutions to the Site Clustering Problem.
nfaffc7fba25c: Human infrastructures are among the most impactful wildlife threats. Although estimates of animal mortality by these structures exist over a given period, they typically do not account for several levels of imperfect detection (i.e. difference between recorded and true mortality). Consequently, true mortality rates may be severely underestimated, as well as their impact on populations and species. We present a hierarchical Bayesian latent‐state modelling framework that sequentially accounts for three processes that produce imperfect detection in estimating mortality abundance: the probability that a hit animal dies on the surveyed area (carcass location probability), the probability that the carcass remains on the surveyed area until the survey is conducted (carcass persistence probability) and the probability that the carcass is observed during the survey process (carcass observation probability). We employ a simulation study where we test the effects of variability in species characteristics, sampling design, latent‐state parameters and prior information on the ability of our model to estimate mortality abundance on roads as total number of roadkills. We then apply our framework to a case study to estimate the total number of roadkills per km in Mediterranean ecosystems while evaluating the cross‐efficiency of different sampling methods. Our framework accurately recovers the total number of roadkills from simulated census data for most simulation scenarios. We detected the highest disagreement between modelling outcomes and simulated data when variability in simulated carcass persistence probability was high and Bayesian priors were highly diffuse. In the case study, our results show notably high roadkill numbers (e.g. estimating 48.92 per km passerines based on 8.04 observed counts), along with substantial variation across different vertebrate groups. Furthermore, our case study confirms that walking and cycling surveys outperform driving surveys in carcass observation rate and provide complementary information, observing partially distinct sets of species and carcass sizes. Our modelling framework offers an efficient approach to estimate mortality rates for a wide range of taxa. Optimizing application requires extensive fieldwork for estimation and integration of imperfect detection. We provide a checklist to help managers assess when infrastructure‐related mortality can be assessed most robustly to prioritise conservation efforts. Resumen Las infraestructuras humanas se encuentran entre las amenazas más impactantes para la fauna silvestre. Aunque existen estimaciones de la mortalidad animal causada por estas estructuras durante un periodo determinado, normalmente no tienen en cuenta los distintos niveles de detección imperfecta (es decir, la diferencia entre la mortalidad registrada y la real). En consecuencia, las tasas reales de mortalidad pueden subestimarse gravemente, así como su impacto sobre las poblaciones y las especies. Presentamos un marco de modelización jerárquico bayesiano de estados latentes que tiene en cuenta secuencialmente tres procesos que generan detección imperfecta al estimar la abundancia de mortalidad: la probabilidad de que un animal atropellado muera en el área muestreada (probabilidad de localización del cadáver), la probabilidad de que el cadáver permanezca en el área muestreada hasta la realización del muestreo (probabilidad de persistencia del cadáver) y la probabilidad de que el cadáver sea observado durante el proceso de muestreo (probabilidad de observación del cadáver). n979c07d62513: Hundreds of thousands of peer‐reviewed articles and grey‐literature reports appear each year in ecology and conservation, creating a pressing need for scalable synthesis tools. We demonstrate that transformer‐based Large Language Models (LLMs), when embedded within a practical, expert‐in‐the‐loop pipeline, offer a reliable path forward requiring no deep AI expertise. In this study, we benchmark nine high ranking LLMs (five standard and four reasoning‐enhanced) across four context‐aware prompting strategies from Basic zero‐shot to advanced Directive formats to extract structured fields (study location, biome, taxa) from abstracts. Our results reveal that while certain models emerge as top performers across the tested fields, no single LLM dominates every task. However, context‐rich prompting drives gains across all models. By mapping API latency, token costs and F1 score, we show how researchers can select the optimal model–prompt pairing for their speed, budget or performance needs. We also provide actionable guidelines for effective context engineering in prompts and validation workflows that build trust in model outputs. To lower the barrier to entry, we also introduce LitStructLLM, a cross‐platform desktop application that lets users upload CSV or PDF inputs, tailor prompts and export reliable, schema‐compliant outputs without writing code. This work underscores the synergy of human expertise and LLM capabilities, offering a robust, transparent pipeline for efficient, large‐scale literature mining in ecology and conservation.
n6c9f265fb681: Understanding the structure and dynamics of deep‐ocean communities requires effective sampling of pelagic organisms in near‐bottom waters. These dispersive organisms contribute to biodiversity, connectivity and ecosystem recovery. Yet, current sampling methods remain constrained by size, cost, and depth, leaving key questions unanswered in complex and remote habitats such as hydrothermal vents, submarine canyons and the hadal zone. To address these limitations, we developed DeepZoo, a compact and cost‐effective ($15,500) autonomous sampler designed for collecting dispersive zooplankton and benthopelagic juveniles at any ocean depth. Powered by a Blue Robotics T200 thruster and a rechargeable lithium polymer battery, DeepZoo filters water through a user‐selectable mesh‐size net (here, 63 μm) for up to 24 h. Lightweight (6.4 kg in water) and portable, the system can be deployed from a range of stationary and mobile platforms. As proof of concept, DeepZoo was field‐tested during two expeditions: (1) at the 9°50′ N East Pacific Rise hydrothermal vent field alongside a McLane pump, and (2) in the Mar del Plata Submarine Canyon off Argentina. DeepZoo was deployed 12 times (878–3780 m) across four platforms, including landers, the HOV Alvin and the ROV SuBastian. The system recovered fauna from 20 taxonomic groups, including gastropod and bivalve veligers, cold‐water coral planulae and cyprid barnacles, in suitable condition for downstream morphological and molecular identification. Together, these results demonstrate DeepZoo as an accessible tool for sampling zooplankton and benthopelagic biodiversity across complex deep‐ocean habitats using both stationary and mobile deployment platforms. By enabling reliable and comparatively affordable collection, DeepZoo expands sampling capacity into environments previously constrained by cost and logistical barriers, supporting biodiversity and connectivity studies in the deep ocean.
na37c00838606: Isotopic mixing models are powerful tools in ecology for estimating diets. Since their initial formulation, these models have evolved into two distinct branches: Bayesian mixing models and dynamic mixing models. Bayesian mixing models significantly improve uncertainty management but remain static assuming a stable state. In contrast, dynamic mixing models are deterministic and incorporate isotopic dynamics, making them suitable for non‐stable systems. However, they lack uncertainty management. To bridge these two approaches, we developed a Bayesian dynamic mixing model. This model integrates isotopic temporal dynamics with robust uncertainty management. In this study, we confronted our model and existing dynamic mixing model to simulations and real‐world case studies. The results revealed that the Bayesian dynamic model outputs exhibit high stability with respect to data variability. It can also partially compensate for inaccuracies in isotopic turnover rate inputs, leading to more reliable diet estimations. This framework provides an accessible and reliable method for conducting diet studies using stable isotopes regardless of the system stability.
n8b7f458aac07: Hidden Markov models (HMMs) are powerful tools for modelling time‐series data with underlying state structure. However, selecting appropriate parametric forms for the state‐dependent distributions is often challenging and can lead to model misspecification. To address this, P‐spline‐based nonparametric estimation of state‐dependent densities has been proposed. While offering great flexibility, these approaches can result in overly complex densities (e.g. bimodal) that hinder interpretability. We propose a method that builds on shape‐constrained spline theory to enforce unimodality in the estimated state‐dependent densities through enforcing unimodality of the spline coefficients. This constraint strikes a practical balance between model flexibility, interpretability, and parsimony. Through three simulation studies and a real‐world case study using narwhal (Monodon monoceros) dive data, we demonstrate the proposed approach yields more stable estimates compared to fully flexible, unconstrained models, thus improving model performance and interpretability. Our method bridges a key methodological gap by providing a parsimonious HMM framework that balances the interpretability of parametric models with the flexibility of nonparametric estimation. This powerful tool allows researchers to derive ecologically meaningful inference from telemetry data while avoiding the pitfalls of overly complex models.
nf3f2fc17aa3b: Formal undergraduate research experiences (UREs) have provided students with authentic research experiences in ecology for decades, but accessibility to these resources is inherently limited, as evidenced during the COVID‐19 pandemic. Moreover, UREs often do not reflect the diversity of locations of current ecological publications. Open online educational resources (OERs) can address the need for more accessible resources, but they usually rely on the curation of static content and can be functionally restricted by a lack of pedagogical instructions. The OCELOTS network (Online Content for Experiential Learning of Tropical Systems) addresses these gaps by shifting the OER model from static curation to a dynamic, scalable ‘incubator matrix’. Rather than serving as a passive repository for disconnected teaching files, OCELOTS acts as a structured workshop and collaborative peer review network where active researchers translate their own peer‐reviewed primary literature into modular, narrative‐driven OER case studies, hereafter referred to as ‘modules’. A combination of factors contributes to OCELOTS' novelty. (a) Researchers who published the study are part of the module‐creating team. (b) Modules are place‐based and globally networked and designed for any type of instructional setting. (c) Peer review is conducted through a living collaborative model rather than a static editorial review. (d) Embedded real‐time data tools use applications that incorporate actual field datasets collected by the module authors. (e) Instructors publish implementation plans and teaching notes for using modules in undergraduate courses. (f) The design is explicitly decolonial in its multilingual accessibility. We summarize the various ways in which 29 OCELOTS modules, representing the work of 68 authors in various tropical field sites in 12 countries, have been created, implemented, adapted, and disseminated. We reflect on how this network has enabled these activities that portray a range of scientific content, processes, and methods in an immersive way. Moving beyond the limitations of standard static text portals, the OCELOTS network presents a highly transferable methodological framework. It demonstrates how global research coordination networks can actively create, review, and implement high‐quality interactive open materials that democratize complex biological data across diverse institutional types around the world.
n32088e7e383b: Long‐read amplicon sequencing is now routine for fungal metabarcoding, and locating the internal transcribed spacer (ITS) subregions within reads has become a throughput bottleneck. Existing extractors were designed for shorter reads and for datasets in which near‐identical sequences are common, and neither assumption holds for Oxford Nanopore or PacBio HiFi amplicons. Extraction failures are also reported opaquely, leaving users unable to distinguish a primer‐design problem from a parameter one. We present ITSxRust, an ITS extractor written in Rust. It delimits regions with a four‐anchor chain across the SSU 3′ end, both 5.8S boundaries and the LSU 5′ start, and falls back to two‐anchor pairs when a read lacks one or two flanks, so that every extracted region retains two profile‐HMM boundaries rather than a read edge. It emits per‐read confidence labels, structured failure codes and a per‐sample QC summary, and provides Nanopore and HiFi parameter presets. We benchmarked it against ITSx and ITSxpress v2 on two Nanopore datasets amplified with different primer pairs. Extraction rates depended strongly on amplicon design. On an ITS1/ITS4 library, ITSxRust recovered 75.3% of reads as full ITS against 69.9% for ITSx, but 76.3% as ITS1 against 93.8%. On an NS5/LR6 library of 54 taxa the ITS1 difference fell to 0.5 percentage points and the full ITS advantage persisted at 2.4. The shortfall is a property of the primer pair: ITS1/ITS4 leaves a median 30 bp of SSU against a 45 bp profile model, so the anchor cannot be matched in full. Where ITSx reported a higher ITS1 yield, 98.3% of the extra reads were ones it had itself flagged as lacking an SSU boundary, retaining a median 30 bp of SSU. Runtime was within 1% of a bare nhmmer search on both datasets, and 6.2 to 9.0 times faster than ITSx. ITSxRust makes the cause of extraction failure visible and quantifiable, which lets users act on primer design rather than guess. It is available under the MIT licence, packaged for Bioconda and Docker, and integrated into nf‐core/ampliseq. Resumen La secuenciación de amplicones de lectura larga es ya rutinaria en el metabarcoding fúngico, y localizar las subregiones del espaciador transcrito interno (ITS) dentro de las lecturas se ha convertido en un cuello de botella de rendimiento. Los extractores existentes fueron diseñados para lecturas más cortas y para conjuntos de datos en los que abundan las secuencias casi idénticas, y ninguno de esos supuestos se cumple en amplicones de Oxford Nanopore o PacBio HiFi. Además, los fallos de extracción se informan de manera opaca, lo que impide al usuario distinguir un problema de diseño de partidores de uno de parámetros. Presentamos ITSxRust, un extractor de ITS escrito en Rust. Delimita las regiones mediante una cadena de cuatro anclajes que abarca el extremo 3′ de la SSU, ambos límites del 5.8S y el inicio 5′ de la LSU, y recurre a pares de dos anclajes cuando una lectura carece de uno o dos flancos, de modo que toda región extraída conserva dos límites definidos por perfiles HMM en lugar de un borde de lectura. Emite etiquetas de confianza por lectura, códigos de fallo estructurados y un resumen de control de calidad por muestra, y ofrece ajustes preestablecidos para Nanopore y HiFi. Lo comparamos con ITSx e ITSxpress v2 en dos conjuntos de datos Nanopore amplificados con distintos pares de partidores. Las tasas de extracción dependieron fuertemente del diseño del amplicón. En una biblioteca ITS1/ITS4, ITSxRust recuperó el 75,3% de las lecturas como ITS completo frente al 69,9% de ITSx, pero el 76,3% como ITS1 frente al 93,8%. En una biblioteca NS5/LR6 de 54 taxones, la diferencia en ITS1 se redujo a 0,5 puntos porcentuales y la ventaja en ITS completo se mantuvo en 2,4. El déficit es una propiedad del par de partidores: ITS1/ITS4 deja una mediana de 30 pb de SSU frente a un modelo de perfil de 45 pb, por lo que el anclaje no puede alinearse por completo.…
n8a207f11c3b6: Identifying individual animals from vocalizations is an emerging research area in computational bioacoustics. This non‐invasive approach reduces reliance on physical capture and tagging for wildlife monitoring. Recent advances in this area leverage deep learning and bioacoustic foundation models adapted from species‐level classifiers. However, these models typically rely on fixed‐window inputs and may not fully capture temporal structure across extended or complex songs, which can contain information relevant to individual discrimination. Here, we evaluate whether modelling sequences of pretrained bioacoustic embeddings improves acoustic individual identification. We developed a framework that integrates transfer‐learned spectrotemporal representations from BirdNET with a lightweight long short‐term memory network. Unlike static baselines that use either the first embedding or an average over all embeddings, our approach processes time‐ordered embedding sequences, allowing the classifier to use information distributed across multiple windows. We evaluated the system using 87,865 vocalizations from 352 individuals across 7 species. We used four publicly available vocalization datasets with individual‐level labels, covering durations from 0.76 s (short calls) to 27.6 s (prolonged songs). Across five random seeds with stratified partitions, the framework achieved mean test accuracies between 93.9% and 98.3% and macro‐F1 scores ranging from 93.2% to 98.3%, without data augmentation. The clearest gains over the strongest static baseline were observed for the great tit and the great spotted kiwi, reaching +1.3 and +2.8 percentage points, respectively. Our results indicate that the contribution of temporal sequence modelling depends on vocalization structure, rather than providing uniform evidence that chronological order drives performance. The benefit of recurrent aggregation was limited or absent for short calls but evident for long vocalizations with multiple informative windows. By combining bioacoustic foundation models with lightweight recurrent modelling, this approach provides a scalable, CPU‐efficient tool for autonomous wildlife monitoring, particularly for species with extended or structurally complex vocalizations. Resumen La identificación de individuos en animales a partir de sus vocalizaciones es un área emergente de investigación en bioacústica computacional. Este enfoque no invasivo reduce la dependencia de la captura física y del marcaje en el monitoreo de la fauna silvestre. Los avances recientes en este campo aprovechan las capacidades del aprendizaje profundo y de los modelos bioacústicos fundacionales adaptados de clasificadores a nivel de especie. Sin embargo, estos modelos suelen utilizar entradas con ventanas de duración fija y pueden no captar por completo la estructura temporal presente en cantos prolongados o complejos, que pueden contener información relevante para la discriminación entre individuos. En este estudio evaluamos si el modelado de secuencias de embeddings bioacústicos preentrenados mejora la identificación acústica de individuos. Desarrollamos un marco de trabajo que integra representaciones espectrotemporales obtenidas mediante aprendizaje por transferencia a partir de BirdNET con una red ligera de memoria a corto y largo plazo (LSTM por sus siglas en inglés). A diferencia de las estrategias estáticas que utilizan únicamente el primer embedding o el promedio de todos los embeddings, nuestro enfoque procesa secuencias de embeddings ordenadas temporalmente, lo que permite al clasificador aprovechar la información distribuida a lo largo de múltiples ventanas. Evaluamos el sistema con 87,865 vocalizaciones de 352 individuos pertenecientes a 7 especies. Utilizamos cuatro conjuntos de datos de vocalizaciones disponibles públicamente y con etiquetas a nivel de individuo, con duraciones que abarcaron desde 0.76 s en llamadas cortas hasta 27.6 s en cantos prolongados.…
nd5e465d13b83: Tools for more efficiently managing agricultural production and the use of limited water resources are required in the context of a growing global population, while the increasing threat posed by droughts and wildfires necessitates improved methods for risk assessment, forecasting and early warning. Quantifying leaf water content is central to these challenges. However, traditional gravimetric measurements are labour-intensive and time-consuming, limiting the assessment of spatial variation, and are not appropriate for all environments due to their destructive nature. We investigate low-cost transmittance meters for rapid non-destructive assessment of leaf water status, making use of radiative transfer simulations and dehydration experiments to test their theoretical and real-world sensitivity to leaf water content. Radiative transfer simulations demonstrate that a transmittance-based meter operating at 940 and 1450 nm is ideally suited to the assessment of leaf water status. Dehydration experiment results reveal strong relationships between the logarithm of the ratio of transmittance at 940 and 1450 nm (as measured with a low-cost transmittance meter) and both equivalent water thickness (r 2 ≥ 0.85) and fuel moisture content (r 2 ≥ 0.81). Our results highlight the potential of low-cost transmittance meters, assembled using inexpensive and readily available components, for rapid non-destructive assessment of leaf water status. Such meters have strong potential to provide valuable information on crop water availability and wildfire risk.
ndc26823defb7: Dispersal is a complex ecological process that can be driven by the abiotic environment, density‐dependent processes and species mobility. Traditionally, dispersal has been studied with capture‐based data that are often limited in space and time. More recently, spatial dynamic N‐mixture models (i.e. N‐mixture models accounting for dispersal among local populations and changes in abundance over time) allow the study of dispersal with count data. However, current spatial dynamic N‐mixture models focus mainly on distance‐based dispersal, limiting our ability to evaluate realistic patterns and drivers of dispersal at relevant spatial and temporal scales. We developed a spatially realistic dynamic N‐mixture model that allows dispersal to be driven by environmental conditions and population density. Using simulations, we evaluated the inferential performance of this model when large proportions of sites are unsurveyed and the survey period is short, situations that are typical of real‐world studies. We then used two case studies to illustrate the applications of this model, one representing a species with limited mobility in fragmented habitat (Chiricahua Leopard Frogs, Lithobates chiricahuensis, in isolated ponds) and the other representing a species with great mobility in continuous heterogeneous habitat (Common Nighthawks, Chordeiles minor, in grasslands). Our simulation study showed that the model provides valid inference even when the number of surveyed sites is small (n=10) or when the survey period is short for dynamic models (5 years), indicating that the model could have great practical value in real‐world studies. The case study of Chiricahua Leopard Frogs showed that the model is capable of revealing pond‐type‐specific dispersal and predicting dispersal among ponds. The case study of Common Nighthawks showed the ability of the model to reveal the effect of primary productivity on dispersal and to map dispersal across the study area. Our effort demonstrates the potential of using count data to gain insights about complex yet realistic dispersal processes. The model that we introduce is flexible and adaptable for a broad range of situations in population and conservation ecology.
n55dcfd927c46: Methodological advances in ecology enable more efficient data collection, yet researchers need to clearly and consistently report the ways in which these methods benefit their own research within the context of their specific needs. Here, we advocate for greater standardization and transparency when assessing new ecological data collection methods. We identify four core evaluation categories: data quantity, data quality, impacts on study systems, and resources, each with sub‐criteria to guide method assessment. As a proof of concept, we review the 2022 volume of Methods in Ecology and Evolution. While most studies focus on data quantity (29/51) and quality (41/51), fewer have stated objectives related to impacts to study systems (6/51) and resource demands (11/51). In cases where the latter are addressed, consequences from impacts and which resources are most limiting vary between field, genetic, and computational approaches. We propose adopting a formalized framework for method evaluation to improve transparency, facilitate informed decision‐making, and enhance the comparability of methodological innovations across ecological studies. Resumen Avances metodológicos de ecología permiten la recopilación de datos más eficiente, sin embargo, los investigadores necesitan informar de forma clara y consistente las maneras que estos métodos benefician sus propias investigaciones en el contexto de sus necesidades específicas. Aquí, abogamos por más estandarización y transparencia en la evaluación de nuevos métodos de recopilación de datos ecológicos. Identificamos cuatro categorías de evaluación centrales: cantidad de los datos, calidad de los datos, impactos sobre los sistemas de estudio, y recursos, cada una con subcriterios para guiar la evaluación del método. Como prueba de concepto, revisamos el volumen de 2022 de Methods in Ecology and Evolution. Mientras que la mayoría de los estudios se centran en la cantidad (29/51) y calidad de los datos (41/51), pocos declaran objetivos relacionados con los impactos en los sistemas de estudio (6/51) y demanda de recursos (11/51). En los casos en que se abordan estos últimos, las consecuencias de los impactos y cuáles recursos son más limitantes varían entre enfoques de campo, genéticos, y computacionales. Nosotros proponemos adoptar un marco formalizado para evaluación de métodos para mejorar la transparencia, facilitar la toma de decisiones informadas, y aumentar la comparabilidad de las innovaciones metodológicas a través de estudios ecológicos.
nbb7fab2af331: Thermal traits are central to understanding how ectotherms respond to environmental warming. However, not all thermal traits describe the same biological process. Critical thermal maxima quantify physiological failure, whereas preferred temperatures describe thermal selection under choice conditions. Voluntary thermal maximum (VTMax) instead captures the body temperature at which an individual voluntarily withdraws from a progressively heated environment. Here, we treat VTMax as a behavioural upper thermal avoidance threshold, rather than as a direct proxy for physiological thermal limits or preferred temperature. We present VTMaxBox, a low‐cost, modular, 3D‐printable practical tool designed to quantify voluntary upper thermal avoidance in terrestrial ectotherms. The system consists of a controlled heating chamber, an escape zone, thermocouples and continuous temperature recording. This design allows researchers to record body temperature at the moment of voluntary withdrawal while controlling heating rate and monitoring internal chamber conditions. We describe the construction, assembly, calibration and scaling of the VTMaxBox and provide open‐source design files to facilitate replication and adaptation. We also outline a recommended experimental workflow, including animal acclimation, chamber stabilization, heating‐rate control, endpoint definition and data extraction. In doing so, we distinguish the hardware itself from the broader experimental protocol required to generate comparable VTMax estimates. We further discuss the performance, limitations and appropriate applications of the VTMaxBox. The tool is best suited for terrestrial ectotherms large enough to carry or contact a thermocouple without major restriction of movement, and small enough to experience stable and homogeneous heating within the chamber. Its use requires careful standardization of chamber size, ramping rate, animal handling and ethical safeguards. VTMaxBox offers an accessible and reproducible platform for incorporating behavioural thermal avoidance into comparative thermal ecology, conservation physiology and teaching. By complementing, rather than replacing, approaches based on critical thermal limits or preferred temperatures, it provides a practical route for studying how animals behaviourally respond to increasing heat exposure under controlled conditions. Resumo Os atributos térmicos são fundamentais para compreender como os ectotermos respondem ao aquecimento ambiental. No entanto, nem todos os atributos térmicos descrevem o mesmo processo biológico. As temperaturas críticas máximas quantificam a falha fisiológica, enquanto as temperaturas preferenciais descrevem a seleção térmica em condições nas quais o indivíduo pode escolher entre diferentes temperaturas. O máximo térmico voluntário (VTMax), por sua vez, corresponde à temperatura corporal na qual um indivíduo abandona voluntariamente um ambiente submetido a aquecimento progressivo. Neste estudo, tratamos o VTMax como um limiar comportamental superior de evitação térmica, e não como uma medida direta dos limites térmicos fisiológicos ou da temperatura preferencial. Apresentamos a VTMaxBox, uma ferramenta prática, modular, de baixo custo e passível de impressão 3D, desenvolvida para quantificar a evitação voluntária de temperaturas elevadas em ectotermos terrestres. O sistema é composto por uma câmara com aquecimento controlado, uma zona de escape, termopares e um sistema de registro contínuo da temperatura. Esse desenho permite registrar a temperatura corporal no momento da saída voluntária do animal, ao mesmo tempo que possibilita controlar a taxa de aquecimento e monitorar as condições internas da câmara. Descrevemos a construção, a montagem, a calibração e o dimensionamento da VTMaxBox, além de disponibilizarmos arquivos de projeto de acesso aberto para facilitar sua reprodução e adaptação.…
ndd0a0734f242: Maximum body size is a key trait of an animal species, determining its population dynamics, productivity and interactions with other species and the environment. For fish in particular, the maximum body length or Lmax correlates strongly to other life history parameters and is commonly used in ecological models and population assessments. Lmax of a species is typically defined as a single value, representing the single largest observed individual or an average of several of the largest individuals. This approach, however, does not explicitly account for sampling effort, where greater sampling intensity generally leads to a higher probability of finding a larger individual, particularly for indeterminate growers. Here we present an R package for Bayesian estimation of maximum animal body size and its uncertainty using the largest observed individuals from multiple samples. Although developed for maximum body length, the method could be applied to estimate other extremes (e.g. greatest body weight, tallest height) from other taxa that grow indeterminately. The package uses three alternative methods—extreme value theory and two versions of exact finite sample approach. The latter two are suitable in cases where the underlying population body‐size distribution can be approximated by a truncated normal distribution. To demonstrate the application of the method we used a hypothetical fishing competition data, but any other records of maximum observed individuals across multiple comparable samples (scientific surveys, trophy hunting, underwater surveys, historical accounts) are also suitable.
n4c56cb342a8d: Habitat connectivity is critical for the conservation of endangered and endemic species, and conversely, it can hinder efforts to contain the spread of harmful biological agents. Here, we introduce geohabnet: a general, spatially explicit, network‐based R package for evaluating, estimating and mapping landscape connectivity from continuous habitat surfaces. The package integrates habitat suitability maps with commonly used dispersal models to evaluate the relative importance of habitat locations to the potential spread of an organism. By incorporating a range of geographic parameters, geohabnet offers a scalable approach to assessing multi‐scale habitat connectivity. Furthermore, geohabnet enables sensitivity analysis across geographic, habitat and network‐metric parameters to quantify uncertainty in habitat connectivity when information about an organism is incomplete, as for emerging diseases or invasive species. To demonstrate geohabnet's functionality, we use publicly accessible plant data to assess habitat connectivity for species that depend on plant hosts, such as plant pathogens, pests and pollinators across Africa and the Americas. geohabnet provides a quick, open‐source, reproducible and generalizable approach to evaluating potential scenarios for the spread of a species through habitat landscapes. By mapping habitat connectivity, geohabnet can support biosecurity and conservation programs, including the design of surveillance strategies for transboundary pathogens, biological invasions and endangered species. Resumen La conectividad del hábitat es fundamental para la conservación de especies endémicas y en peligro de extinción, pero también puede obstaculizar los esfuerzos de contener la propagación de agentes biológicos nocivos. En este estudio se presenta geohabnet: un paquete en el programa R para evaluar, estimar y catografiar la conectividad de las especies a partir de superficies continuas de hábitat, basado en un modelo general de redes geográficas. El paquete integra mapas de idoneidad del hábitat con modelos de dispersión de uso común para evaluar la importancia de distintas áreas de hábitat en la propagación potencial de un organismo. Al incorporar una amplia gama de parámetros geográficos, geohabnet ofrece un enfoque escalable para evaluar la conectividad de las especies a múltiples escalas. Además, geohabnet permite realizar análisis de sensibilidad de parámetros geográficos, de hábitat y de métricas de red para cuantificar la incertidumbre en las estimaciones de conectividad cuando la información sobre un organismo es incompleta, como ocurre con las enfermedades emergentes o las especies invasoras. Para demostrar la funcionalidad de geohabnet, se utilizaron datos públicos sobre cultivos en África y el continente americano, evaluando así la conectividad para especies que dependen de hospedantes vegetales, tales como plagas, enfermedades y polinizadores. geohabnet proporciona un enfoque rápido, de código abierto, reproducible y generalizable para evaluar escenarios potenciales de propagación de una especie a través de áreas con hábitat. Mediante el mapeo de la conectividad del hábitat, geohabnet puede ser de apoyo para los programas de bioseguridad y conservación, incluyendo el diseño de estrategias de vigilancia para plagas transfronterizas, especies invasoras y en peligro de extinción.
n2fe2e7617d20: Biodiversity–ecosystem functioning (BEF) experiments seek to improve predictions of how biodiversity change affects ecosystem functioning. Bridging biodiversity change research with BEF experiments can accelerate these efforts. Diverse observational and experimental approaches for detecting and attributing biodiversity changes offer opportunities to re-analyze data from existing BEF experiments and design new ones. This integration helps us examine the effects of all biodiversity-change scenarios—species loss, gain, and turnover. We propose a mechanistic framework for experiments that manipulate both biodiversity and environmental conditions. The framework reveals how environment-driven biodiversity changes alter ecosystem functioning by identifying how species identity and interactions separately affect ecosystem functions. Integrating the fields of biodiversity change and BEF improves our understanding of the causes and functional consequences of biodiversity change.
n9f571a3f2de7: Biodiversity loss is considered a major global issue, but at the same time, scientists interpret it differently, identifying varied drivers, solutions, and responsibilities in their published works. These interpretations shape the scientific narratives these scientists use to discuss biodiversity loss, which, in turn, affects policy through the biodiversity science–policy interface. However, a comprehensive overview of these different narratives within biodiversity loss literature is lacking. To address this gap in knowledge, we conducted a literature review of contemporary, global biodiversity literature and a discursive network analysis based on biodiversity loss drivers, solutions, and responsibilities. We identified seven narratives that represent an overview of the scientific discourse on biodiversity loss. We determined that the narratives identify different key drivers of biodiversity loss and often focus primarily on either drivers, solutions, or responsibilities, whereas some neglect societal dimensions. Moreover, our research showed that the commonly used Intergovernmental Science–Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES) categorization of direct drivers of biodiversity loss is reflected in only one of the seven narratives, thereby indicating its limited prevalence across the literature. Thus, this study will help biodiversity scientists develop more holistic biodiversity loss narratives by recognizing the limitations of the narratives they currently use. Additionally, our findings can assist policymakers in identifying relevant but less common narratives in the biodiversity science–policy literature that may help them develop policies. El discurso científico de la pérdida de biodiversidad presentado con factores, soluciones y responsabilidades Resumen La pérdida de biodiversidad se considera un problema mundial de gran importancia, pero, al mismo tiempo, los científicos la interpretan de forma diferente, pues identifican diversos factores causales, soluciones y responsabilidades en sus trabajos publicados. Estas interpretaciones dan forma a las narrativas científicas que se utilizan para abordar la pérdida de biodiversidad, lo que a su vez influye en las políticas a través de la interfaz entre la ciencia y la política en materia de biodiversidad. Sin embargo, no existe una visión general completa de estas diferentes narrativas en la bibliografía sobre la pérdida de biodiversidad. Para llenar este vacío de conocimiento, realizamos una revisión bibliográfica de la literatura contemporánea y global sobre biodiversidad, así como un análisis de redes discursivas basado en los factores causales, las soluciones y las responsabilidades de la pérdida de biodiversidad. Identificamos siete narrativas que ofrecen una visión general del discurso científico sobre la pérdida de biodiversidad. Determinamos que las narrativas identifican diferentes factores clave de la pérdida de biodiversidad y, a menudo, se centran en los factores causales, las soluciones o las responsabilidades, mientras que algunas descuidan las dimensiones sociales. Además, nuestra investigación mostró que la categorización de los factores directos de la pérdida de biodiversidad, comúnmente utilizada por la Plataforma Intergubernamental Científico‐Normativa sobre Diversidad Biológica y Servicios de los Ecosistemas (IPBES), sólo se refleja en una de las siete narrativas, lo que indica su limitada prevalencia en la literatura. Por lo tanto, este estudio ayudará a los científicos especializados en biodiversidad a desarrollar narrativas más holísticas sobre la pérdida de biodiversidad, al reconocer las limitaciones de las narrativas que utilizan actualmente. Además, nuestros resultados pueden ayudar a los responsables políticos a identificar narrativas relevantes, aunque menos comunes, en la literatura científica y política sobre biodiversidad, que puedan servirles para elaborar políticas.
n9cb7b234e33e: Mammalian reproductive and glandular systems provide multiple routes through which maternal microorganisms can be transmitted to offspring, yet the evolutionary significance of these pathways remains incompletely understood. This manuscript proposes that mammalian evolution progressively incorporated microbial transmission into reproductive biology, increasing the fidelity with which beneficial host-associated microorganisms pass between generations. Under this framework, mammary glands evolved from ancestral apocrine-like glands to create sustained maternal–offspring interfaces through which microbial transmission could become an additional selectable function when host–microbe associations enhanced fitness. Comparative evidence from monotremes, marsupials, and eutherian mammals is examined through an apocrine–mammary–microbiota axis, encompassing glandular regulation of epithelial microbial communities, maternal microbial transmission during birth and lactation, and host mechanisms that selectively support microbial establishment. The term filial microorganism is introduced to distinguish microbial lineages whose intergenerational transmission is facilitated by evolved host mechanisms from microorganisms that are merely transmitted through maternal contact or environmental exposure. The framework is further extended, more speculatively, to the eutherian placenta, which is proposed to function not as a resident microbial reservoir but as a transient immunological interface capable of initiating low-abundance microbial founder populations during the physiological transition from pregnancy to birth. Subsequent exposure through the birth canal, maternal skin, glandular secretions, and lactation may then expand and refine these populations during early development. This hypothesis predicts that candidate filial lineages should exhibit preferential maternal transmission, persistence across host generations, evidence of host mechanisms facilitating their maintenance or transfer, and measurable contributions to host fitness. If supported, this framework would broaden mammalian inheritance beyond the transmission of host genes to include evolved biological mechanisms that preserve beneficial microbial partnerships across generations.
nd7a7aeda39a7: Roads affect wildlife through multiple pathways, including changes in abundance, activity, mortality, habitat use, and movement, yet these responses have rarely been synthesised within a common evidence framework. We fitted separate three-level meta-analytic models to 643 effects from 160 studies. On the log-response-ratio scale, road proximity was associated with approximately 32% lower wildlife outcomes (lnRR = −0.3872, 95% CI [−0.7293, −0.0452]). The standardized mean-difference estimate ( g = −0.1131, 95% CI [−0.2608, 0.0346]) and correlation-based estimate ( Z = 0.1691, 95% CI [−0.1915, 0.5297]) were both imprecise. Response-type patterns varied across metric families, indicating that road effects are expressed through distinct ecological pathways rather than as a uniform shift in all wildlife outcomes. Between-study heterogeneity was substantial, and prediction intervals included both reductions and increases across sites. Annual average daily traffic was available for 91 of the 643 analysed effects, representing 17 studies. Overall, roads were associated with heterogeneous wildlife responses, with the clearest average reduction observed on the ratio scale. More consistent reporting of traffic volume and road characteristics is needed to test transferable dose–response relationships.
n96723f693250: Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog. Abstract Climate change and intensified fire regimes are reshaping ecosystems globally. Reptiles, as ectotherms, rely on microhabitat shelters to buffer against thermal extremes, yet the capacity of these shelters to persist or function following fire remains poorly understood. As heatwaves and fire regimes intensify under climate change, effective thermal buffering will become increasingly vital for reptile persistence. This study quantifies how fire alters the structure and thermal offset of key reptile refugia: spinifex (Triodia) tussocks, chenopod shrubs, and leaf‐litter mats, in the dune and swale habitats of South Australia's Murray Mallee. Using iButton data loggers deployed across four fire histories, we measured hourly microhabitat and adjacent ground temperatures, modelling thermal offset (Toffset) via mixed‐effects models. More recent fire histories were associated with less spinifex and leaf‐litter cover and more bare ground, although evidence for changes in individual shelter dimensions was mixed. Thermal buffering declined markedly in recently burnt sites, with long‐unburnt spinifex providing the greatest daytime protection from extreme ground temperatures. Structural properties such as tussock height and litter depth were associated with Toffset, supporting a relationship between shelter structure and thermal‐refuge quality. Comparisons with the thermal tolerance of spinifex‐obligate reptiles indicate that burnt habitats often exceed critical thermal limits, effectively eliminating usable refugia during heatwaves. These results demonstrate that fire‐driven structural simplification translates to weakened thermal refugia, with implications for species persistence under increasing heat extremes. Effective fire management in arid systems should, therefore, prioritise the protection and regeneration of long‐unburnt spinifex and litter habitats as critical microclimatic refuges.
